common_name: Perle von Nurnberg Echeveria (Iridescent Purple-Pink Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Perle von Nurnberg requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water, especially in the center of the rosette, which quickly leads to rot.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Perle von Nurnberg is a classic hybrid echeveria prized for its large, iridescent rosettes of dusty mauve-purple leaves with a pearlescent pink-lavender sheen that shifts subtly with the light, one of the most striking color combinations among ornamental echeveria hybrids. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings, and it makes an excellent container or rock garden specimen in the warm, dry conditions it prefers. In zone 9a it can be grown outdoors in a well-drained container or bed but should be moved under cover or indoors during hard freezes, since it has little cold tolerance.

common_name: Alice du Pont Mandevilla (Classic Vigorous Pink Mandevilla)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm, training the twining vine onto a trellis, arbor, or fence; Alice du Pont is one of the oldest and most vigorous mandevilla cultivars, producing large, clear pink, trumpet-shaped flowers over glossy foliage.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a trellis, arbor, or other support able to accommodate a vigorous twining vine. Alice du Pont is a long-established classic mandevilla cultivar, valued for producing large, glossy, deep green leaves and abundant clear pink, trumpet-shaped flowers continuously from late spring through fall, with a naturally vigorous, fast-climbing habit compared to some of the more compact modern mandevilla series. It thrives in the heat and humidity of a Gulf South summer, needing only regular water and monthly fertilizing during active growth. In zone 9a it typically dies back after a hard freeze but often regrows from the roots in a mild winter; in colder zones it is best grown as a container plant brought indoors or treated as an annual.

common_name: California Gold Bougainvillea (Golden-Orange Vigorous Tropical Vine)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; California Gold produces vivid golden-orange papery bracts on a vigorous, thorny climbing vine that needs a sturdy support and thrives on somewhat neglectful, dry conditions.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun on a strong, permanent trellis, arbor, or wall, since mature vines become heavy and woody over time. California Gold produces masses of vivid golden-orange papery bracts, the true flowers being the small white blooms tucked inside, covering the vigorous, thorny vine through the warm season, especially heavily when the plant is kept on the dry, slightly stressed side, since bougainvillea blooms more prolifically with somewhat restricted water and root space than when pampered. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and is one of the more cold-hardy bougainvillea colors for the warmer parts of zone 9, though hard freezes will still cause dieback that regrows from the roots in spring.

common_name: String of Hearts (Rosary Vine, Chain of Hearts)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright indirect light to partial sun; String of Hearts is typically grown as a hanging basket or trailing container plant rather than in the ground, since it has very little cold tolerance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial sun, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings. String of Hearts produces long, thin, trailing stems draped with small, heart-shaped, marbled gray-green and silver leaves, occasionally accented with a pink or purple blush, making it a favorite hanging basket and shelf plant that cascades gracefully over a container edge. It is a true succulent and rots quickly in overly wet, poorly drained soil, so err on the side of underwatering, particularly in winter when growth slows. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container that can be moved indoors or under cover during freezes, since it has very little cold tolerance, unlike more cold-hardy garden succulents.

common_name: Marble Queen Pothos (Heavily Variegated White-Green Pothos)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light to partial shade; Marble Queen has heavier white variegation than standard golden pothos, which slows its growth rate and makes it need somewhat brighter light to maintain vigor.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial shade, protected from direct hot sun which can scorch the pale variegated portions of the leaves. Marble Queen is a striking pothos cultivar with heart-shaped leaves marbled in bold patches of creamy white and green, a much more heavily variegated form than standard golden pothos, though the extensive white patches mean it grows more slowly and needs brighter light to stay vigorous and avoid reverting to plain green. It trails or climbs readily and is a popular hanging basket, shelf, or totem-trained houseplant, tolerating average indoor conditions and irregular watering better than most houseplants. In zone 9a it can summer outdoors in a shaded spot but must come indoors well before frost, since it has no cold tolerance.
